constraint_a: Deliberately repeat the same key words many times in your response. Do NOT use synonyms -- always reuse the exact same words. For example, if you mention 'energy', keep saying 'energy' every time, never switch to 'power' or 'force'. Repetition of words is strongly required. Every sentence should reuse the main topic words.
constraint_b: Never repeat any content word more than once in your entire response. Always use a different synonym each time. For example, say 'important' once then switch to 'crucial', 'vital', 'significant', 'essential', 'key', 'critical'. Maximize word diversity -- each sentence must use completely new vocabulary.

verifier.description: Computes content-word repetition density: 1 - (unique_content_words / total_content_words) after filtering stop words. High score = repetitive, low score = diverse. The inverted scorer returns 1 - density. Threshold T=0.216 separates: density >= T means repetitive (followed constraint_a), density < T means diverse (followed constraint_b).

root_causes.description: Responses with moderate repetition of a single dominant topic word (e.g., 'war' x6 in 27 words, 'magnetic' x4 in 20 words) fall below the density threshold because the remaining vocabulary is varied. The aggregate density metric dilutes concentrated single-word repetition when the response also contains many unique words.

Same mechanism as a_to_b: response repeats 'freelancing' x5 and 'employment' x5 in 38 content words but overall density (0.211) barely misses threshold 0.216 because many other words are unique. The model clearly attempted deliberate repetition.

recommended_action: None. The 3 misclassifications (0.12%) are inherent to the aggregate density metric treating all content words equally rather than weighting concentrated topic-word repetition. The wide optimal range [0.053, 0.377] means no threshold adjustment would fix these borderline cases without introducing new errors on the other side. The verifier is fundamentally sound; the error rate is negligible for downstream Phase 1 probing.

rubric.text: Classify as followed_a if the response deliberately reuses the same content words multiple times, creating noticeable repetition of key topic terms throughout the text. The hallmark is that the writer avoids synonyms and instead hammers the same words sentence after sentence. Classify as followed_b if the response uses diverse vocabulary with minimal word reuse, employing synonyms and varied phrasing so that few content words appear more than once. If a response repeats a single unavoidable topic word (like a proper noun) a few times but otherwise uses rich, varied vocabulary, classify based on the dominant pattern: if the response reads as deliberately repetitive in strategy, classify as followed_a; if it reads as naturally diverse with incidental topic-word reuse, classify as followed_b. Classify as followed_neither only if the response is off-topic or incoherent.

notes: All 2500 condition C responses are clean content with zero refusals, zero meta-commentary. The model never refuses or comments on the constraint conflict -- it simply picks a strategy and executes it.
The model strongly favors following the system instruction (98.2% followed_system), consistent across both directions (98.3% a_to_b, 98.0% b_to_a).

The 3 misclassified responses all share the same root cause: a single topic word is repeated 4-6 times, but the surrounding vocabulary is varied enough to keep aggregate density below threshold. This is an inherent limitation of the aggregate density metric, not a verifier bug.

The score distribution is strongly bimodal: most responses are either very repetitive (>0.5 density, N=1477) or very diverse (<0.1 density, N=18 in a_to_b + ~1200 in b_to_a as 1-density). The grey zone [0.1, 0.3) contains only 19 responses total, making threshold placement non-critical.

Short responses (< 10 content words) appear only in b_to_a direction, all with density 0.0 (perfectly diverse). These are correctly labeled followed_system. The model produces terse, synonym-rich responses when following the diverse constraint.
The optimal range [0.053, 0.377] is very wide, confirming the bimodal separation. The per-model threshold 0.216 sits comfortably in the middle with no feasibility concerns.
Words like 'diverse' (37 hits) and 'repeat' (10 hits) appear in responses as genuine content vocabulary, not meta-commentary about the instructions.
